sources.title: Major Dhyan Chand Singh (Q381138), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-28): label 'Major Dhyan Chand Singh', description 'Indian field hockey player (1905-1979)', born 29 August 1905, died 3 December 1979, Korean label present, image 'Dhyan Chand closeup.jpg'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Olympedia, 'Dhyan Chand' athlete profile (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: three Olympic hockey golds with India in 1928, 1932 and 1936, centre-forward, called there the greatest hockey player ever; 8 goals against the United States in 1932, 3 against Germany in the 1936 final; still the star of the Indian team in 1947-48 but declined selection for 1948. Olympic statistical reference with an admiring tone.

Boria Majumdar and Nalin Mehta, extract from 'Olympics: The India Story' published as 'The World's Best Centre-Forward' on Outlook India (read in full): Amsterdam 1928, with contemporary Statesman match reports quoted, saying he scored 14 of India's 29 goals and that in one match he set up others rather than improve his own goal average; also his own recollection that the England-withdrawal story was hearsay. Scholarly book extract.

ThePrint profile, 'Dhyan Chand: the hockey wizard who refused Hitler's offer to join German Army' (read in full, 2019): career outline, the 1936 warm-up loss and squad changes, the Indian team playing without shoes in the final, a lost tooth, 61 goals in 22 matches on his last tour at 43, a fellow Olympian's recollection of his humility, and the Hitler offer reported as belief. Journalistic profile, partly based on his autobiography.

DT Next, 'Dhyan Chand's Berlin Saga: Captaincy test in Nazi Germany, Hitler myth' (read in full, 2021): his first Olympic captaincy in 1936, worry after a loss before the Games, a Statesman report saying he was past his best, rubber-soled shoes in the Japan match, funding from princely rulers, and a closing statement that scholars call the Hitler army-offer story an urban myth. Critical journalism, partly drawing on his autobiography.

Scroll.in, 'National Sports Day: Dhyan Chand on chasing Olympic glory, being snubbed and meeting Don Bradman' (read in full): excerpts from his autobiography 'Goal' on the 1928 departure, playing the final with a fever and the 'Do or Die' slogan. Self-report, used only as a minor supplement and never as sole support.
Wikimedia Commons file pages 'Dhyan Chand closeup.jpg' and 'SLNSW 81891 Indian captain Dhayan Chand taken in Sydney in August 1935' (checked for the portrait only; not used for any scoring).

persistence.rationale: [src_dhyan_olympedia, src_dhyan_theprint, src_dhyan_scroll | 1926-1948 | Olympic reference + journalistic profile + self-report] Olympedia dates his first international tour to 1926 and his golds to 1928, 1932 and 1936, and says he was still the star of the Indian team in 1947-48; ThePrint says he scored 61 goals in 22 matches on the December 1947 East Africa tour aged 43 and lost a tooth in a rough 1936 final; his own account in Goal (via Scroll) says he played the 1928 final with a high fever. The span of top-level play is well documented, but the hardship details are largely self-reported or retold and no independent account of his training habits was read.

adaptability.rationale: [src_dhyan_theprint, src_dhyan_dtnext | 1936 | journalistic profiles] ThePrint says that after a 4-1 warm-up loss to Germany in 1936 he made a couple of changes to the squad and the team resumed winning, and that the players switched to playing without shoes in the final; DT Next instead says he chose rubber-soled shoes in the Japan match for speed and mobility. The two retellings of the footwear episode disagree on detail and may repeat one legend, so only the general willingness to change the team's set-up is supported. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 62 / 0.45 to 58 / 0.40 because the footwear episode is retold with conflicting details in two journalistic retellings of one legend.

collaboration.rationale: [src_dhyan_majumdar, src_dhyan_olympedia | 1928-1936 | scholarly extract quoting contemporary press + Olympic reference] A Statesman report from the 1928 Games, quoted by Majumdar and Mehta, says that against Belgium he tapped the ball to teammates rather than push his own goal tally, and the same extract says he scored 14 of India's 29 goals; Olympedia notes that he played alongside his younger brother Roop Singh in 1932 and 1936. The contemporary report is a single match description, so the row is modest and rests on one quoted article.

portrait.reason: No rights-clear portrait resolved. Wikidata image 'Dhyan Chand closeup.jpg' (211 x 350) has no known photographer, and its Commons page cites only a 2008 English Wikipedia upload and a hockey-fan website with a generic India public-domain tag. The alternative checked, a 5 August 1935 Sam Hood photograph in the State Library of New South Wales collection (Commons file 'SLNSW 81891', 763 x 1050, Australian public domain, created before 1955), has a clear rights basis but the library's own record says the sitter was identified by a Flickr user in 2012, and other frames of that sitting are captioned only 'Indian hockey team', so the sitter's identity is not established. Next step: find a photograph with a documented identification of the sitter, for example a captioned Trove newspaper photograph of 1935 or an Olympic-era press photograph with a named photographer, or confirm the identification with the State Library. Kind, if resolved: likeness.
